title: How to Use Gua Sha: Face and Body Steps, Angle and Pressure — cv.cm
description: How to use gua sha on the face and body: tool edges, a 15° angle, oil, stroke direction, passes per area, what the red sha marks are and who should avoid it.
h1: How do you use gua sha on your face and body?
answer: Apply oil, hold the tool almost flat (about 15° for the face), and pull it in one direction with light, slow strokes, 5–10 passes per area. On the face, use light pressure that leaves no marks. Traditional body gua sha uses firmer strokes on the back and shoulders and often leaves red marks (sha). Skip it on broken skin and ask a doctor first if you take blood thinners.

sections.h: Two different practices with one name
body: Gua sha (刮痧, pronounced "gwah shah") means "scraping sha" in Chinese. Today the name covers two quite different things, and it helps to keep them apart.

ul: Facial gua sha is a modern beauty routine. A smooth stone or metal tool glides over oiled skin with light pressure. The aim is a relaxing self-massage. It should not leave marks.

Body gua sha is a traditional East Asian folk technique, known in Vietnam as cạo gió and also as coining or spooning. A tool with a rounded edge is stroked firmly over oiled skin, usually on the back, neck sides and shoulders, until red or purple marks called sha appear.

body: In traditional Chinese medicine, gua sha is described as moving qi and blood. These are traditional concepts, not physiology. What researchers can measure is a short-term rise in blood flow in the skin and, in a few small trials, short-term changes in pain. Both are covered below.
This guide is for adults using gua sha on themselves, or gently on a family member or friend. It is not medical advice.

sections.h: The tool: shapes, edges and preparation
body: Most tools are flat pieces of jade, rose quartz, other stone, stainless steel, horn or ceramic. Traditional households also use a porcelain soup spoon or a coin. The material matters less than the edge.

head: Part of the tool
What it looks like
Use it for
rows: Cheeks, jaw line, sides of the neck, shoulders and back
Along the jaw bone and around the forearm or calf
Two small bumps with a dip between them
Jaw line and the area below the cheekbone, on the face only
Small areas such as beside the nose and under the brow bone, very lightly

body: Before each use, check the edge with a fingertip. A chip or crack can cut the skin, so replace a damaged tool. Wash it with warm water and mild soap and dry it. Wash your face or the body area too.

Always use oil or a slippery lotion or serum. A dry tool drags and irritates the skin. Use enough that the tool glides without catching: for the face, about 3–5 drops of a plain facial oil; for the upper back, about half a teaspoon of plain massage or cooking oil warmed in the hands.

sections.h: How to do facial gua sha step by step
body: Hold the tool nearly flat against the skin, at about 15° from the surface, so a wide part of the edge touches. Use light pressure, about 2–3 out of 10: the tool moves the skin, not the muscle below. Pull the tool in one direction only, up and outward, then lift it off and start again. Do not saw back and forth. Use your free hand to hold the skin steady at the start of each stroke if it pulls.

ol: Neck sides (30 s per side): stroke down from just below the ear to the collarbone, on the side of the neck only. Never stroke the front of the neck or the throat. 5 passes.
Jaw line (30 s per side): place the notched edge on the jaw bone at the chin and pull back toward the ear. 5–8 passes.
Cheeks (30 s per side): place the long edge beside the nose, under the cheekbone, and pull outward toward the ear. 5–8 passes.

Under the eyes (15 s per side): with the rounded tip and the lightest pressure, glide from the inner corner outward along the bone of the eye socket to the temple. Stay on the bone. Never press on the eyeball. 3 passes.
Brows (15 s per side): glide from the inner end of the brow outward along the brow bone. 3–5 passes.
Forehead (30 s): stroke up from the brows to the hairline, working from the center outward. 5 passes per strip.

body: The whole routine takes about 5 minutes. A little pinkness that fades within 10–20 minutes is normal. Redness that lasts, small dots, or any pain mean you pressed too hard. Two to four times a week is plenty. If you want to time each area, a timer such as cv.cm's countdown keeps you from overdoing one spot.

sections.h: How traditional body gua sha is done
body: Traditional body gua sha is usually given by a trained practitioner, or by a family member at home in many parts of Asia. The person sits or lies face down, and the oiled skin is stroked with a rounded edge held at about 30–45° from the skin.

rows: Downward, in strips about 3 cm from the spine on each side, never on the spine itself
10–20 strokes per strip, medium pressure (4–5 out of 10)

body: Each stroke is slow, about 1–2 seconds long, and in one direction. In the traditional method, stroking continues in one strip until red spots appear or the color stops changing, and then the giver moves on. At home there is no need to aim for marks. Light to medium strokes that leave the skin pink are enough for a relaxing session, and they carry less risk.

Keep away from the spine, the shoulder blade edges and other bony points, the front of the neck, the armpit, moles, and any spot that hurts sharply. Ask the person often whether the pressure is comfortable. Discomfort that feels good is fine. Sharp, stinging or burning pain means stop.

The red to purple marks after body gua sha are petechiae and small bruises: tiny spots of bleeding under the skin from broken small blood vessels (capillaries). They are not "toxins" or "bad blood" coming out, even though folk explanations sometimes say so.
In most people the marks are not painful and fade on their own within a few days. Keep the area warm and covered, and do not repeat gua sha on the same area until the marks have fully faded.

body.note: Small red dots or bruises that appear without gua sha or an injury are a different matter. Unexplained spots, spots that spread quickly, or spots with fever or feeling unwell need a doctor promptly.

body: Facial gua sha should never leave these marks. If it does, you used too much pressure or too sharp an edge.
Research on gua sha is small and of limited quality, and almost all of it is on body gua sha, not facial gua sha.

ul: A 2007 pilot study in 11 healthy adults used laser imaging and found that one gua sha session on the back raised blood flow in the surface tissue about fourfold for the first few minutes, with a smaller rise for the rest of the 25-minute measurement.

A 2011 randomized trial in 48 adults with long-term neck pain found that one gua sha session reduced neck pain over one week more than a heat pad did. The trial was small and not blinded, and the authors said long-term value was not known.
There is no good evidence that facial gua sha permanently lifts, slims or reshapes the face, removes wrinkles, or drains the lymph system. Any puffiness change after a session is temporary.

body: A fair summary: many people find gua sha relaxing, and small studies suggest short-term pain relief for neck pain, but the evidence is limited. Gua sha is not a treatment for any disease. Neck or back pain that is severe, lasting, or comes with other symptoms needs a proper medical check.

sections.h: Safety: who should avoid it and when to stop
body: Do not use gua sha, on the face or body, over:

ul: broken, cut, infected or sunburned skin, rashes, active acne, eczema or psoriasis flares, or rosacea that is inflamed
fresh bruises, recent injuries, swelling, or a recent surgical scar
varicose veins, moles, skin growths, or any lump you have not had checked

body: Ask a doctor before trying body gua sha, and use only light facial strokes or none, if you:

ul: take blood thinners such as warfarin, apixaban, rivaroxaban, heparin, or daily aspirin, or have a bleeding or clotting disorder
have a history of blood clots, poor circulation, diabetes, or fragile or thin skin
are having cancer treatment such as chemotherapy (gentle touch is often fine; the care team should decide)
are pregnant, have a fever, or feel unwell

body: Stop and see a doctor if you notice bruising much larger or darker than expected, marks that do not fade within about two weeks, skin that becomes hot, swollen or oozing (possible infection), or new numbness or weakness in the arms. Neck pain after a fall or accident, or neck stiffness with fever and headache, needs urgent medical care, not gua sha.

body: After each use, wash the tool with warm soapy water, rinse, dry it, and store it in a clean case. Do not boil or soak stone tools for long, as some stones can crack.

faq.a: No. Facial gua sha should feel like a light, smooth glide. Body gua sha can feel firm and slightly uncomfortable, but sharp, stinging or burning pain means you should stop.

faq.q: How often should I do facial gua sha?
faq.a: Two to four times a week for about 5 minutes is enough for most people. If your skin stays red or feels sore, use it less often and more lightly.

faq.q: Can gua sha get rid of a double chin or slim the face?
faq.a: There is no good evidence that gua sha removes fat or changes face shape permanently. Some people notice that puffiness looks less for a short time after a session.

faq.q: How long do gua sha marks last?
faq.a: Marks from body gua sha usually fade on their own within a few days. If they last longer than about two weeks, or you bruise easily, see a doctor.

faq.q: Is cạo gió the same as gua sha?
faq.a: Cạo gió is the Vietnamese name for a very similar folk scraping practice, often done with a coin and oil. The same safety points apply, including avoiding it with blood thinners or broken skin.

faq.q: Should I use gua sha in the morning or at night?
faq.a: Either is fine. Many people use it in the evening as part of winding down, while others use it in the morning. Clean skin, oil and light pressure matter more than the time of day.
